          Clásico Win, Sky-High Team Spirit, and Real Madrid in the Title Race: José Mourinho is Back
        
      
                          
                      Oct 26, 2026
          
                      Ali Tweedale / Author
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Against the odds, José Mourinho took Real Madrid to Camp Nou and came away with a much-deserved win. The title race is on in La Liga.
Sunday’s Clásico wasn’t quite, well, a classic, in the context of this storied fixture’s history.
But it was still an encapsulating affair from start to finish, largely because this was two high-quality teams, both of whom went all out to win the match.

In normal circumstances, José Mourinho, returning to this fixture for the first time in more than 13 years, might have set up not to lose. After Raphinha’s equaliser on the hour mark, there might have been a flurry of substitutions to shut up shop and avoid a loss that would have opened up a surely unassailable nine-point gap to Barcelona.

But the Real Madrid manager knew even a draw here wasn’t really enough. A win was needed to close the gap to three points and breathe life into a title race that, given Barcelona had won La Liga for the last two seasons and Madrid had lost two of their opening seven games, threatened to turn into a procession before we even reached November.

But in the face of all that pressure and widespread doubts about his suitability for another role at one of the biggest clubs in the world because he hasn’t won a league title since the 2014-15 Premier League with Chelsea, the 63-year-old stood up. There was nothing about Madrid’s performance at Camp Nou, where Barcelona had not failed to win a single game since their return there a year ago, that suggested any fear of losing.

Mourinho proved his doubters categorically wrong with a daring display of attacking intent and a fully deserved win that extended his unbeaten run in Clásicos to six games (W4 D2) in all competitions. He is only the third Madrid manager ever to achieve that feat, after Miguel Muñoz (1962-1965) and Vicente del Bosque (2001-2003).

He is a different person and different manager these days, but this win was classic Mourinho. There was a full acknowledgement of the quality their opponents possessed and little attempt to beat them at their own game: Madrid had just 37.8% of the ball and their threat was almost entirely based around swift, direct breaks upfield.

Madrid put together four direct attacks – quick breaks up the pitch that end with a shot or a touch in the opposition’s box – against Barcelona on Sunday night. That is two fewer than Barcelona’s first nine opponents in La Liga had managed combined (six) this season. Madrid progressed up the pitch an average of 15.1 metres with each passing sequence, which was by far the most anyone has managed against Barça this season.

They did this almost exclusively through the wide areas, playing almost no passes straight through the middle of the pitch, but instead getting the ball out to Arda Güler on the right or, more often, Yan Diomande on the left to drive forwards before either shooting or putting a low ball across goal.

Both Madrid goals came from balls into the channel: first for Diomande to chase and square for Kylian Mbappé (via a big slice of luck through a failed Gerard Martín clearance) and later for substitute Eduardo Camavinga to race down the right and pull the ball back for Mbappé's 87th-minute winner.

Mourinho has always meticulously tailored his game plans depending on the opponent, and he is clearly not doing things any differently these days. There was an awareness that Lamine Yamal would not track back as hard as another winger might, and a focus on attacking down that flank as a result. Madrid had 45.4% of their attacking touches down the left flank.

The teenage Diomande, who has grown into his role since his big-money summer move, was a constant threat, shining once again in the absence of the suspended Vinícius Júnior, who, as it happens, may not have worked as hard without the ball as his understudy. After this display, it will be fascinating to see how Mourinho handles the Brazilian's return given there’s certainly an argument they have looked a more complete team without him. Two-goal match-winner Mbappé insisted afterwards that this was “a team victory”.

“If we want to achieve things this year, we have to do it as a group and as a team because the quality is here,” he said. “When you see the players we have, anyone who says there’s no quality is lying. But we have to do everything as a team and as a group because that’s how we’re going to achieve the things we want to achieve.”

The collective endeavour showed a level of buy-in to what Mourinho is doing that bodes well for a team who have gone two years without winning a single major trophy – since Mbappé signed, coincidentally or not. The last time they went three years without one, Mourinho was still enjoying his first spell at Chelsea.

There was also the inevitable sprinkling of underhanded play that was always going to be present for a Mourinho-led Madrid team playing in a Clásico, with two players who joined alongside him this summer front and centre.

Marc Cucurella was tasked with keeping Spain teammate Yamal quiet and he largely did an exceptional job, although fouls were a common sight. He made the joint-most fouls of any player on the pitch (four), along with the other main protagonist, Bernardo Silva.

Silva was handed his first start in La Liga since 12 September and was a cool, calming presence in front of the Madrid defence, a big-game player who was in no way overawed by the magnitude of the occasion, completing 91.7% of his passes while also breaking up play well, legally or not.
Perhaps most impressive about either of Cucurella or Silva’s performances was the fact they played a combined 170 minutes and both avoided bookings.

Madrid and Mourinho will know they need to be sensible. They can’t glean too much from this single result. They remain three points off top spot and are even still behind city rivals Atlético in the table, too. There’s loads of work still to be done.
